label: copy-phase input c (fed-back c), not on the final step
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase, when the fed-back input token is c, i.e. the model is re-reading a c it just emitted (in_tok=c accounts for 99.4% of activation mass, and nothing fires in the original or delimiter phases). It is strongest when the c is the first original token, so the step right after <DEL> (recall_idx 1) carries the top activations, around 4.4 to 4.8; c at later copy positions gives weaker activations, typically 0.1 to 1.5 relative to max 4.77. Firing is weaker or absent when the c is the last copy input (to_go = 0), in short sequences, and often on a second, repeated c. It essentially never fires on other tokens, and never on c during the original phase. Simple predicate phase==2 & in_tok==c: dev F1 0.78, mass recall 0.99; excluding the final step raises F1 to 0.82.

issues: The core label holds. Every activation is in the copy phase (dev mass share copy = 1.000, original = 0, delimiter = 0), and in_tok=c carries 99.4% of the mass. Max is 4.766, and the top examples are all c as orig(0), fed back at recall_idx 1.

The claim that firing is 'weaker or absent when the c is the last copy input (to_go = 0)' is wrong for long sequences. For L=9, recall_idx=8 (to_go=0), the firing rate on c is 0.638 (n=2721), which is higher than the rate at L=9, r=5 (0.51). The predicate's (to_go >= 1) clause stands in for a length-by-position effect. It is not really a final-step effect.

Systematic false-positive class: whether c fires is graded by position and length, and the predicate does not capture this. Firing rate on copy-phase c: L=3 r=1 0.24, L=3 r=2 0.00; L=4 r=3 0.00; L=5 r=3 0.48; L=6 r=5 0.13; L=7 r=5 0.30, r=6 0.13; L=9 r=4..8 0.51-0.64. Against that, r<=3 with L>=6 fires 0.88-1.00. About 25% of predicted steps are inactive (18.5k FPs on test). They are not scattered noise. They concentrate on c in the last two or three copy slots of short and medium sequences, and on mid/late slots generally.

The claim that firing is 'often absent on a repeated second c' is confounded with position. A repeated c (an earlier c already fed back) fires 0.514 vs 0.667 overall. Restricted to recall_idx<=3 and L>=6, it is 0.979 vs 0.982, so there is no real difference.
The explanation's 'later copy positions typically 0.1 to 1.5' is roughly right. The quartile examples show c at r=2-3 with relative activation 0.1-0.3, which is about 0.5-1.4.
Scores reproduce: dev P 0.753, R 0.911, F1 0.8245, mass recall 0.973. The simpler predicate phase==2 & in_tok==c gets F1 0.783 and mass recall 0.994, as reported.
